explanation.whyCorrect: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates unconjugated bilirubin with glucuronic acid, yielding water-soluble conjugated bilirubin that is then actively secreted into the canaliculus and bile.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bilirubin is conjugated, not oxidized by CYP450; CYP450 acts on lipophilic xenobiotics in Phase I detoxification.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduction to urobilinogen occurs in the gut after bile delivery, downstream of biliary secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Albumin binding transports unconjugated bilirubin in plasma before hepatic uptake, not immediately before biliary secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heme oxygenase converts heme to biliverdin in macrophages, upstream of hepatic uptake and conjugation.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis becomes disoriented and asterixic. His arterial ammonia is elevated. In the brain, which reaction underlies the astrocyte swelling and cerebral edema of hepatic encephalopathy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of ammonia to urea within astrocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of ammonia to glutamine within astrocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxidation of ammonia to nitrate by neurons

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conjugation of ammonia with glucuronic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deamination of glutamine releasing ammonia in astrocytes

explanation.summary: Because the failed hepatic urea cycle lets ammonia reach the brain, astrocytes detoxify it to glutamine, an osmotically active solute that drives swelling and cerebral edema.
explanation.whyCorrect: Astrocytes use glutamine synthetase to convert ammonia plus glutamate into glutamine. Glutamine accumulation is osmotically active, causing astrocyte swelling and cerebral edema characteristic of hepatic encephalopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The urea cycle operates in hepatocytes, not astrocytes; its failure is why ammonia reaches the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no meaningful oxidation of ammonia to nitrate in neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucuronidation is a hepatic Phase II reaction for lipophilic compounds, not ammonia detoxification in brain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Deamination of glutamine to release ammonia would worsen, not explain, the protective conversion that causes swelling; the net astrocytic reaction here forms glutamine.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman ingests a large quantity of acetaminophen in a suicide attempt. Hepatocellular necrosis is expected to begin in which acinar zone, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Zone 1, because of high oxygen tension favoring beta-oxidation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Zone 2, because of transitional mixed metabolism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zone 1, because of high urea cycle activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Zone 3, because of high CYP450 activity generating NAPQI

choices.label: E
choices.text: Zone 3, because of high-affinity glutamine synthetase activity

explanation.summary: Zone 3 (pericentral) has the highest CYP450 expression, converting acetaminophen to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, so injury starts there.
explanation.whyCorrect: Zone 3 hepatocytes express the most CYP450 enzymes, which oxidize acetaminophen to NAPQI. NAPQI depletes glutathione and causes oxidative necrosis, making zone 3 the site of earliest injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Zone 1 has high oxygen tension and favors oxidative metabolism, but it is relatively spared in acetaminophen toxicity because it has less CYP450.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Zone 2 is transitional and not the site of earliest acetaminophen injury.
whyWrongByChoice.C: High urea cycle activity in zone 1 does not generate NAPQI or explain acetaminophen necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glutamine synthetase activity in zone 3 detoxifies residual ammonia; it is the CYP450-derived NAPQI, not glutamine synthetase, that causes the necrosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is brought in 12 hours after a massive acetaminophen overdose. Which mechanism best explains why N-acetylcysteine is an effective antidote?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It supplies cysteine, the rate-limiting precursor for glutathione synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: It directly inhibits CYP450 oxidation of acetaminophen

choices.label: C
choices.text: It binds NAPQI covalently in the plasma before hepatic uptake

choices.label: D
choices.text: It replaces vitamin K to restore clotting factor activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: It raises plasma oncotic pressure to protect hepatocytes

explanation.summary: NAC replenishes cysteine, the rate-limiting substrate for hepatic glutathione synthesis, restoring the glutathione pool that NAPQI depletes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glutathione, synthesized in the liver from cysteine, glycine, and glutamate, detoxifies NAPQI. NAC provides cysteine, the rate-limiting precursor, replenishing glutathione and neutralizing NAPQI.

whyWrongByChoice.B: NAC's principal benefit is glutathione repletion, not direct CYP450 inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NAC does not act primarily by binding NAPQI in plasma; NAPQI is generated intracellularly in hepatocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin K and clotting factors are unrelated to NAC's antioxidant mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NAC does not work by raising oncotic pressure; that is a property of albumin.

questions.stem: A researcher labels hepatocytes near the terminal portal venule (zone 1) in a healthy liver. Compared with pericentral hepatocytes, these periportal cells are expected to show the highest activity of which pathway?

explanation.summary: Zone 1 periportal hepatocytes receive oxygen-rich blood and preferentially perform oxidative pathways such as gluconeogenesis, beta-oxidation, and urea synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Zone 1's high oxygen tension favors energy-demanding oxidative processes, so gluconeogenesis, beta-oxidation, and urea synthesis predominate there.

whyWrongByChoice.A: De novo lipogenesis is a zone 3 (pericentral) function.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycolysis predominates in zone 3, the lower-oxygen pericentral region.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CYP450 biotransformation is concentrated in zone 3.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glutamine synthesis via high-affinity glutamine synthetase is a zone 3 function scavenging residual ammonia.

questions.stem: A patient undergoes surgical resection of 60% of the liver for a tumor. Within hours, the initiation phase of regeneration begins. Which stimulus best characterizes this earliest phase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: TGF-beta and activin suppressing hepatocyte division

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatic progenitor cells in the canals of Hering differentiating into hepatocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: HGF binding MET to drive DNA replication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Kupffer cell–derived TNF-alpha and IL-6 with increased sinusoidal shear stress priming hepatocytes from G0 to G1

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stellate cell activation producing collagen scar

explanation.summary: Regeneration initiation is driven by hemodynamic shear stress and Kupffer-derived cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6) that prime quiescent hepatocytes to enter the cell cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: After resection, increased sinusoidal shear stress and Kupffer cell–derived TNF-alpha and IL-6 prime hepatocytes, moving them from G0 into G1 (the priming/initiation phase).

whyWrongByChoice.A: TGF-beta and activin terminate regeneration (the hepatostat), the opposite of initiation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HGF/MET signaling drives the proliferation phase that follows priming, not the earliest initiation event.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Progenitor cell activation occurs mainly when hepatocyte proliferation is impaired, not in normal initiation after resection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stellate cell collagen production produces fibrosis, not the initiation of physiologic regeneration.

questions.stem: During liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy, hepatocytes complete one to two rounds of replication and then stop once the original liver-to-body mass ratio is restored. Which signaling pair mediates this termination ('hepatostat')?

explanation.summary: TGF-beta and activin suppress hepatocyte proliferation once the appropriate liver mass is restored, terminating regeneration.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hepatostat terminates regeneration through TGF-beta and activin, which inhibit further hepatocyte division after the liver-to-body mass ratio is normalized.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HGF and EGF are mitogens driving proliferation, not termination.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TNF-alpha and IL-6 prime hepatocytes in the initiation phase, not termination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Wnt/beta-catenin establishes zone 3 identity; it is not the termination signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Notch/Jagged influences cholangiocyte and progenitor fate, not the hepatostat termination signal.

questions.stem: A hepatologist explains why a patient with advanced cirrhosis cannot regenerate functional liver after an acute insult, despite intact HGF and IL-6 signaling. Which factor best accounts for the failure of effective regeneration?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Overproduction of HGF flooding MET receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrous architectural distortion impairing hepatocyte repopulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excess albumin synthesis crowding out hepatocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids

explanation.summary: In cirrhosis, fibrosis and distorted architecture prevent orderly hepatocyte repopulation, so regeneration produces disorganized nodules rather than functional tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cirrhotic fibrous septa and architectural distortion physically impair hepatocyte repopulation; regenerative nodules are disorganized repair attempts rather than restoration of function, even when mitogenic signaling is intact.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Kupffer cells are present in cirrhosis; their absence is not the mechanism of regenerative failure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HGF overproduction does not explain regenerative failure; signaling is described as intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Albumin synthesis is reduced, not increased, in cirrhosis, and it does not crowd out hepatocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of enterohepatic bile acid recycling does not explain the failure of hepatocyte repopulation in cirrhosis.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman is found to have low serum hepcidin and iron overload. Recognizing hepcidin as a hepatocyte-derived hormone, which action explains its role as the master regulator of systemic iron homeostasis?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It oxidizes iron to Fe3+ for loading onto transferrin

choices.label: C
choices.text: It transports iron in plasma as Fe3+

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stores intracellular iron as a soluble complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: It increases ferroportin expression to enhance iron absorption

explanation.summary: Hepcidin lowers systemic iron availability by binding ferroportin and triggering its degradation, blocking iron export into plasma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepcidin binds ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages and causes its internalization and degradation, decreasing dietary iron absorption and iron release. Low hepcidin therefore permits unchecked iron export and overload.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Oxidation of iron to Fe3+ is the ferroxidase function of ceruloplasmin, not hepcidin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transferrin, not hepcidin, transports iron as Fe3+ in plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intracellular iron storage is the role of ferritin, not hepcidin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepcidin degrades ferroportin and reduces absorption; it does not increase ferroportin expression.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with cholestatic jaundice from bile duct obstruction has a prolonged PT that fully corrects after parenteral vitamin K. What does this response indicate about his hepatic function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His hepatocellular synthetic capacity is severely and irreversibly lost

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coagulation factor synthesis is intact but vitamin K was unavailable for gamma-carboxylation due to fat malabsorption

choices.label: D
choices.text: He has disseminated intravascular coagulation consuming factors

explanation.summary: Correction of the PT with vitamin K shows synthetic capacity is preserved and the deficiency was substrate-based: cholestasis impaired fat-soluble vitamin K absorption needed to gamma-carboxylate factors II, VII, IX, and X.
explanation.whyCorrect: Factors II, VII, IX, and X require vitamin K–dependent gamma-carboxylation to become active. In cholestasis, impaired bile flow reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K; if the hepatocytes can still synthesize factors, supplying vitamin K restores carboxylation and corrects the PT.

whyWrongByChoice.A: If synthetic capacity were lost (hepatocellular failure), vitamin K would not correct the PT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PT correction addresses clotting factors; it says nothing about albumin having stopped, and does not indicate that.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DIC-consumed factors would not be corrected simply by administering vitamin K.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The PT reflects clotting factor carboxylation, not platelet function.

questions.stem: An investigator studies bile acid economy in a healthy adult and measures the fraction of the bile acid pool that returns to the liver rather than being synthesized anew each cycle. Approximately what fraction is recycled, and by what route?

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 95%, via reabsorption in the terminal ileum and portal return

explanation.summary: Enterohepatic circulation reabsorbs roughly 95% of bile acids in the terminal ileum and returns them to the liver via portal blood, minimizing the synthetic burden.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 95% of the bile acid pool is reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and carried back to the liver through the portal circulation, so only a small fraction must be resynthesized each cycle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bile acids are recycled via the ileum and portal vein, not renal reabsorption, and the fraction is ~95%, not 50%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphatic drainage is not the route, and 20% is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The returning route is the portal vein, not the hepatic artery.
whyWrongByChoice.B: About 95% (not 5%) is recycled, and reabsorption occurs in the terminal ileum, not the colon.

questions.stem: A pharmacologist notes that an orally administered drug undergoes extensive metabolism before reaching the systemic circulation, sharply reducing its bioavailability. This first-pass effect depends on which anatomic feature of hepatic blood supply?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The hepatic artery delivering oxygenated systemic blood directly to zone 3

choices.label: B
choices.text: The portal vein delivering gut-absorbed drug to hepatocytes before systemic distribution

choices.label: C
choices.text: The central vein draining bile into the intestine

choices.label: D
choices.text: The canals of Hering routing drug to progenitor cells

explanation.summary: First-pass metabolism occurs because orally absorbed drug enters the portal vein and passes through the liver before reaching the systemic circulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Substances absorbed from the gut enter portal blood and perfuse the hepatocytes first. Hepatic (and gut wall) metabolism during this initial pass reduces the fraction reaching the systemic circulation, i.e., the first-pass effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The hepatic artery supplies oxygenated systemic blood, but the first-pass effect specifically depends on portal delivery of gut-absorbed drug.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The central vein drains blood toward the vena cava and does not carry bile into the intestine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The canals of Hering house progenitor cells and are not the route for first-pass drug delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no lymphatic pathway that bypasses hepatocytes to explain first-pass metabolism.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old ultramarathon runner has fasted for 20 hours. Hepatic glycogen stores are nearly exhausted, yet plasma glucose remains near-normal. Which hepatic process is now the principal source of blood glucose?

explanation.summary: Once hepatic glycogen is depleted during prolonged fasting, gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol, and amino acids maintains blood glucose.
explanation.whyCorrect: After ~18–24 hours of fasting hepatic glycogen is largely exhausted, so the liver sustains glucose output primarily through gluconeogenesis using non-carbohydrate precursors (lactate, glycerol, amino acids).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycogenolysis dominates early fasting but cannot be the main source once glycogen stores are depleted.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycogenesis stores glucose in the fed state; it does not release glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: De novo lipogenesis consumes glucose to make fat in the fed state; it does not generate blood glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GLUT2-mediated uptake removes glucose from blood in the fed state rather than supplying it.

questions.stem: A toxicologist describes a two-phase hepatic pathway that renders a lipophilic drug water-soluble: first a CYP450-mediated reaction unmasks a reactive group, then a second reaction attaches glucuronate. What is the correct designation of these two steps?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Phase I oxidation followed by Phase II conjugation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phase II conjugation followed by Phase I oxidation

explanation.summary: Detoxification proceeds as Phase I (CYP450 oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis) then Phase II conjugation (e.g., glucuronidation) to produce excretable water-soluble compounds.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phase I biotransformation, primarily CYP450-mediated, introduces or unmasks a reactive functional group; Phase II then conjugates the intermediate with glucuronate, sulfate, glycine, or glutathione to yield a water-soluble excretable product.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The order is reversed; Phase I (functionalization) precedes Phase II (conjugation).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis are glucose pathways, not xenobiotic biotransformation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-oxidation and lipogenesis are lipid pathways, unrelated to drug detoxification phases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Deamination and transamination are amino acid reactions, not the Phase I/Phase II detoxification sequence.

questions.stem: A patient with severe chronic liver disease is noted to have a paradoxical tendency toward both bleeding and thrombosis. Which feature of hepatic synthetic function best explains this coagulation paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only procoagulant factors are synthesized by the liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: The liver synthesizes only anticoagulant proteins such as protein C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coagulation factors are made by the spleen, not the liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: The liver synthesizes both procoagulant and anticoagulant factors, and both decline together

explanation.summary: The liver makes both procoagulant and anticoagulant factors; when synthesis fails, both fall, creating a rebalanced but fragile hemostatic state prone to bleeding and thrombosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatocytes synthesize procoagulants (e.g., factors II, VII, IX, X, fibrinogen) and anticoagulants (e.g., protein C, protein S, antithrombin). In cirrhosis both are lost, producing a precariously rebalanced system that can tip toward either bleeding or thrombosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The liver makes anticoagulant proteins too; the paradox arises precisely because both classes decline.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The liver synthesizes both procoagulant and anticoagulant proteins, not only anticoagulants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Coagulation factors are synthesized in the liver, not the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: In cirrhosis platelet counts typically fall (splenic sequestration, reduced thrombopoietin), not rise.

questions.stem: In a mouse model, hepatocyte proliferation is pharmacologically blocked after toxic injury, yet the liver still regenerates using an alternative cell population. Where do these bipotential reserve cells reside?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The space of Disse among stellate cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Kupffer cell lining of the sinusoids

explanation.summary: When hepatocyte proliferation is impaired, bipotential hepatic progenitor (oval) cells in the canals of Hering activate and can become hepatocytes or cholangiocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatic progenitor cells reside in the canals of Hering. They are bipotential and, when hepatocyte replication is blocked, differentiate into hepatocytes or cholangiocytes to support regeneration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The space of Disse houses stellate cells (vitamin A storage, fibrosis), not the bipotential progenitor reserve.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Central vein endothelium is not the residence of hepatic progenitor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Portal lymphatics do not house the regenerative progenitor population.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kupffer cells are macrophages that help prime regeneration but are not the bipotential progenitors.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with longstanding cirrhosis develops sudden decompensation with jaundice, encephalopathy, and coagulopathy after an acute bacterial infection, and rapidly progresses to multiorgan failure. Which principle best explains why this insult produced catastrophic failure rather than compensated recovery?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute insults never affect chronically diseased livers

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepcidin overproduction caused the multiorgan failure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cirrhotic livers regenerate faster than normal livers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Albumin's long half-life protects against acute decompensation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The chronically injured liver has depleted regenerative reserve, so an acute insult triggers acute-on-chronic liver failure

explanation.summary: Acute-on-chronic liver failure occurs when an acute insult strikes a liver whose regenerative reserve is already exhausted by chronic disease, precipitating rapid decompensation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In established chronic liver disease, fibrosis and progenitor exhaustion deplete regenerative reserve. A superimposed acute insult (e.g., infection) overwhelms the remaining capacity, producing acute-on-chronic liver failure with rapid, often multiorgan, decompensation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronically diseased livers are highly vulnerable to acute insults; this statement is false.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cirrhotic livers regenerate poorly, not faster than normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Albumin's long half-life does not protect against acute decompensation and is irrelevant to this collapse.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepcidin regulates iron homeostasis and does not cause acute-on-chronic multiorgan failure here.

questions.stem: A hepatic surgeon states that safe major liver resection depends on leaving enough functional parenchyma for regeneration. Beyond approximately what proportion of hepatic mass loss does insufficient parenchyma remain, such that spontaneous regeneration may fail and transplantation is required?

explanation.summary: Loss of more than about 70–80% of hepatic mass can leave insufficient parenchyma to regenerate, potentially requiring transplantation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although the liver has remarkable regenerative capacity, loss exceeding roughly 70–80% of hepatic mass may leave too little functional parenchyma to restore mass and function, at which point transplantation may be needed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of only 10–20% is easily regenerated; this is far below the threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 30–40% loss is well within regenerative capacity and is a routine resection burden.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Even 50–60% loss is typically survivable with regeneration; the critical threshold is higher.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Requiring more than 95% loss overstates the threshold; failure risk emerges above roughly 70–80%.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing the regulation of heme biosynthesis. Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting first committed step of the pathway, converting succinyl-CoA and glycine to delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA)?

explanation.summary: ALA synthase catalyzes the rate-limiting, committed first step of heme synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALA synthase condenses succinyl-CoA and glycine to form ALA in the mitochondrion; this is the rate-limiting and regulated step, subject to feedback repression by heme.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferrochelatase catalyzes the final step, inserting Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX, not the first step.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ALA dehydratase acts on the second step, condensing two ALA molecules into porphobilinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Porphobilinogen deaminase acts downstream, forming hydroxymethylbilane from porphobilinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heme oxygenase participates in heme degradation, not synthesis.

questions.stem: All of the carbon and nitrogen atoms of the porphyrin ring are derived from just two small precursor molecules combined at the start of heme synthesis. Which pair is correct?

explanation.summary: Heme's porphyrin ring is built entirely from glycine and succinyl-CoA.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALA synthase combines glycine and succinyl-CoA to form ALA; eight of each ultimately supply all carbons and nitrogens of the porphyrin ring.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neither glutamate nor acetyl-CoA is the direct substrate for ALA synthase in mammals.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serine and malonyl-CoA are used in one-carbon and fatty-acid metabolism, not porphyrin synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alanine and pyruvate are not the porphyrin precursors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glutamine and acetoacetate are unrelated to the first step of heme synthesis.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man being treated for tuberculosis with isoniazid develops a microcytic, hypochromic anemia with ringed sideroblasts. The anemia reflects impaired activity of ALA synthase, whose function depends on a coenzyme derived from which vitamin?

explanation.summary: ALA synthase is a pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6)-dependent enzyme.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALA synthase requires PLP (vitamin B6) as a coenzyme. Isoniazid depletes B6, impairing ALA synthesis and producing a sideroblastic microcytic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B12 deficiency causes macrocytic, megaloblastic anemia and is not the ALA synthase coenzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia; folate is not required by ALA synthase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thiamine is a coenzyme for decarboxylations such as pyruvate dehydrogenase, not ALA synthase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin C aids iron absorption but is not the ALA synthase coenzyme.

questions.stem: In hepatocytes, the intracellular heme concentration tightly controls the flux through the heme biosynthetic pathway. Which mechanism best describes how heme exerts negative feedback on its own synthesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heme increases transcription of ALA synthase to accelerate the pathway

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heme stimulates mitochondrial import of ALA synthase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heme represses ALA synthase transcription and blocks its import into mitochondria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Heme upregulates DMT1 to increase iron uptake

explanation.summary: Heme feeds back to suppress ALA synthase (ALAS1) at multiple levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heme represses ALAS1 transcription, inhibits the enzyme, and blocks import of the ALAS1 precursor into the mitochondrion; it also induces heme oxygenase to promote degradation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heme represses rather than induces ALAS1 transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heme regulation acts chiefly at the ALAS step, not by activating ferrochelatase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heme blocks, not stimulates, mitochondrial import of the ALAS precursor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: DMT1 controls intestinal iron uptake and is not the mechanism of heme feedback on synthesis.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child living in an old home presents with abdominal pain, irritability, and a microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling. A blood lead level is markedly elevated. Lead produces these findings by inhibiting which two enzymes of the heme pathway?

explanation.summary: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lead blocks ALA dehydratase (causing ALA accumulation and neurotoxicity) and ferrochelatase (blocking iron insertion), producing microcytic anemia with elevated protoporphyrin and ALA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates bilirubin and is not a lead target; ALA synthase is not the inhibited enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heme oxygenase and biliverdin reductase are degradation enzymes not inhibited by lead.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Porphobilinogen deaminase and UDPGT are not the classic lead-inhibited enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase is deficient in PCT, not the enzyme pair inhibited by lead.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old boy develops a microcytic anemia. Bone marrow shows ringed sideroblasts with Prussian-blue-positive iron encircling erythroblast nuclei. A defect in which erythroid-specific enzyme most likely explains this X-linked disorder?

explanation.summary: X-linked sideroblastic anemia results from ALAS2 deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALAS2 is the erythroid isoform of ALA synthase. Its deficiency impairs heme synthesis while iron continues to enter mitochondria, forming ringed sideroblasts.

whyWrongByChoice.B: ALAS1 is the housekeeping hepatic isoform, not the erythroid-specific enzyme mutated here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ferrochelatase is decreased (not overactive) in sideroblastic states; the X-linked classic cause is ALAS2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates bilirubin and is unrelated to sideroblast formation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heme oxygenase degrades heme and does not cause sideroblastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of severe diffuse abdominal pain, tachycardia, and confusion. Attacks follow use of certain medications and fasting. There is no photosensitivity, and urine darkens on standing. Urinary porphobilinogen and ALA are markedly elevated. A partial deficiency of which enzyme underlies this condition?

explanation.summary: Acute intermittent porphyria is caused by porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase) causes acute intermittent porphyria, with accumulation of ALA and porphobilinogen, neurovisceral attacks, and no photosensitivity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ALA dehydratase deficiency is very rare and does not fit the classic acute intermittent porphyria PBG elevation pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda with photosensitivity, not neurovisceral attacks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria with photosensitivity, not this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ALA synthase is upregulated during attacks; its deficiency does not cause AIP.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C and heavy alcohol use develops painless blistering and fragility of sun-exposed skin on the dorsal hands, along with hyperpigmentation and tea-colored urine. Which enzyme deficiency best explains the most common porphyria producing this picture?

explanation.summary: Porphyria cutanea tarda results from uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reduced uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity causes porphyria cutanea tarda, the most common porphyria, with photosensitive blistering, skin fragility, and tea-colored urine from uroporphyrin accumulation; hepatitis C and alcohol are classic triggers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria with neurovisceral attacks and no photosensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria with painful (non-blistering) photosensitivity, not this classic PCT picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ALA dehydratase deficiency is a rare acute porphyria without cutaneous blistering.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency causes variegate porphyria, a less common cause than PCT.

questions.stem: The final step of heme biosynthesis occurs in the mitochondrion and completes the mature heme molecule. Which reaction is catalyzed by ferrochelatase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA to form ALA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxidation of protoporphyrinogen IX to protoporphyrin IX

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insertion of ferrous iron (Fe2+) into protoporphyrin IX

choices.label: E
choices.text: Removal of carboxyl groups from uroporphyrinogen III

explanation.summary: Ferrochelatase inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX to form heme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ferrochelatase catalyzes the terminal step, chelating ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX to produce heme; it is inhibited by lead.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA is the first step, catalyzed by ALA synthase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase performs the oxidation to protoporphyrin IX, the step just before ferrochelatase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Porphobilinogen deaminase forms hydroxymethylbilane, an earlier cytosolic step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase removes carboxyl groups earlier in the pathway.

questions.stem: When senescent red blood cells are degraded by splenic macrophages, the heme ring is opened by an enzyme that also produces an endogenous gaseous signaling molecule. Which enzyme performs the first step of heme degradation, converting heme to biliverdin?

explanation.summary: Heme oxygenase converts heme to biliverdin, releasing CO and iron.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heme oxygenase opens the porphyrin ring, forming biliverdin and releasing carbon monoxide and ferrous iron; the CO is the endogenous gaseous product.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biliverdin reductase acts next, reducing biliverdin to unconjugated bilirubin, not converting heme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferrochelatase functions in synthesis, inserting iron rather than degrading heme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates bilirubin later in the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Porphobilinogen deaminase is a synthesis enzyme, not involved in degradation.

questions.stem: Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin is lipophilic and water-insoluble, so it cannot circulate freely in plasma. To which plasma carrier is unconjugated bilirubin bound during transport from macrophages to the liver?

explanation.summary: Unconjugated bilirubin travels bound to albumin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because unconjugated bilirubin is water-insoluble, it binds tightly to serum albumin for transport to the liver, which keeps it from being freely filtered by the kidney.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Transferrin transports iron in plasma, not bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin is inside red cells; it is a source of heme, not the bilirubin carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ceruloplasmin carries copper and has ferroxidase activity, not bilirubin transport.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin, not bilirubin.

questions.stem: Bilirubin must be made water-soluble before it can be excreted in bile. In which location and by which enzyme is unconjugated bilirubin conjugated with glucuronic acid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In splenic macrophages by heme oxygenase

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the bile duct by ferrochelatase

choices.label: E
choices.text: In the intestine by bacterial beta-glucuronidase

explanation.summary: Hepatocyte UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates bilirubin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Within hepatocytes, UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) attaches glucuronic acid to bilirubin, making it water-soluble (direct/conjugated) for excretion in bile.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Macrophages generate unconjugated bilirubin via heme oxygenase and biliverdin reductase; they do not conjugate it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Biliverdin reductase forms unconjugated bilirubin and does not perform glucuronidation in plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ferrochelatase is a synthesis enzyme and does not act in the bile duct.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bacterial beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin in the gut; it does not conjugate it.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man notices mild scleral icterus during a bout of the flu and after fasting for an exam. Physical exam and liver enzymes are normal. Labs show mildly elevated unconjugated bilirubin with a normal conjugated fraction, and no hemolysis. Which condition best explains this benign, intermittent picture?

explanation.summary: Gilbert syndrome causes mild, stress-triggered unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gilbert syndrome is a common, benign condition with mildly reduced UGT1A1 activity, producing intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia precipitated by fasting, illness, or stress, with otherwise normal liver function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crigler-Najjar type 1 presents in neonates with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus, not mild intermittent jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dubin-Johnson causes conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia with a black liver, not mild unconjugated jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rotor syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not an isolated mild unconjugated rise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Biliary obstruction produces conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with pale stools and dark urine and abnormal liver tests.

questions.stem: A newborn develops severe jaundice within the first days of life with markedly elevated unconjugated bilirubin unresponsive to phenobarbital, and is at high risk for kernicterus. Genetic testing shows a complete absence of UGT1A1 activity. Which diagnosis is most consistent?

explanation.summary: Complete absence of UGT1A1 defines Crigler-Najjar type 1.
explanation.whyCorrect: Crigler-Najjar type 1 features a total lack of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity, causing severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from birth, no response to phenobarbital, and high kernicterus risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gilbert syndrome has only mildly reduced UGT1A1 and causes benign, mild jaundice, not life-threatening neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Physiologic jaundice is mild and self-limited, not a complete enzyme absence with kernicterus risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dubin-Johnson causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not severe unconjugated jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rotor syndrome causes a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and is benign.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has chronic mild jaundice with a predominantly conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia and normal liver enzymes. During an unrelated laparoscopy, the liver appears grossly black. This condition is caused by a mutation in a canalicular transporter. Which diagnosis fits best?

explanation.summary: Dubin-Johnson syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with a black liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dubin-Johnson syndrome results from an ABCC2 (MRP2) mutation impairing canalicular excretion of conjugated bilirubin, producing direct hyperbilirubinemia and a grossly black liver from pigment accumulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gilbert syndrome causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and a normal-appearing liver.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Crigler-Najjar type 2 causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not a conjugated pattern with a black liver.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rotor syndrome also causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia but does NOT produce a black liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemolytic anemia produces unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and does not blacken the liver.

questions.stem: A young adult has chronic, mild conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver enzymes. Unlike a related disorder, the liver is grossly normal in appearance, and the defect involves impaired hepatic uptake and storage of conjugated bilirubin due to mutations in SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3. Which diagnosis is correct?

explanation.summary: Rotor syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia without a black liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rotor syndrome results from mutations in SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3 impairing hepatic uptake and storage of conjugated bilirubin; it is benign and, unlike Dubin-Johnson, does not blacken the liver.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dubin-Johnson produces a grossly black liver due to an ABCC2/MRP2 defect, distinguishing it from Rotor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gilbert syndrome causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not a conjugated pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Crigler-Najjar type 1 causes severe unconjugated neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wilson disease causes copper overload with hepatic and neurologic disease, not isolated benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

questions.stem: A jaundiced 4-day-old term infant with elevated unconjugated bilirubin is placed under blue-green phototherapy lights. By what mechanism does phototherapy lower the serum bilirubin level?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It photoisomerizes unconjugated bilirubin into water-soluble forms

choices.label: C
choices.text: It enhances binding of bilirubin to albumin

choices.label: D
choices.text: It suppresses heme oxygenase to reduce bilirubin production

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stimulates erythropoiesis to dilute bilirubin

explanation.summary: Phototherapy isomerizes bilirubin into water-soluble products.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blue-green light (about 460-490 nm) converts insoluble unconjugated bilirubin in skin capillaries into water-soluble photoisomers (and lumirubin) that can be excreted in bile and urine without hepatic conjugation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phototherapy does not act by inducing UGT1A1; it bypasses the need for conjugation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Its mechanism is photoisomerization, not enhancing albumin binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: It does not work by suppressing heme oxygenase or reducing production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stimulating erythropoiesis would not lower bilirubin and is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A severely jaundiced neonate with very high unconjugated bilirubin becomes lethargic and develops abnormal tone and a high-pitched cry, raising concern for permanent neurologic injury. Which property of unconjugated bilirubin accounts for this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is water-soluble and freely filtered by the kidney

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is directly toxic to hepatocytes causing cholestasis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is lipid-soluble and can cross the blood-brain barrier

choices.label: D
choices.text: It precipitates in bile to form pigment gallstones

choices.label: E
choices.text: It binds irreversibly to transferrin and blocks iron delivery

explanation.summary: Lipid-soluble unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier, causing kernicterus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipophilic; when it exceeds albumin binding capacity, it crosses the blood-brain barrier and deposits in the basal ganglia, producing kernicterus and irreversible neurologic damage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Unconjugated bilirubin is water-insoluble and NOT filtered by the kidney; only conjugated bilirubin appears in urine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kernicterus reflects CNS deposition, not hepatocyte toxicity causing cholestasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pigment gallstone formation is a separate downstream phenomenon and does not explain the neurologic injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bilirubin does not bind transferrin; it binds albumin, and this is not the mechanism of brain injury.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic inflammatory disease has a normocytic anemia with low serum iron, low transferrin saturation, but high ferritin. Elevated hepcidin drives this anemia of chronic disease. What is the principal molecular action of hepcidin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases DMT1 to boost enterocyte iron uptake

choices.label: B
choices.text: It stimulates erythropoietin release from the kidney

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reduces ferric iron to ferrous iron for absorption

choices.label: D
choices.text: It binds ferroportin and triggers its internalization and degradation

choices.label: E
choices.text: It increases transferrin synthesis to raise iron-binding capacity

explanation.summary: Hepcidin degrades ferroportin, limiting iron export into plasma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepcidin binds the iron-export channel ferroportin, causing its internalization and degradation. This traps iron in enterocytes and macrophages, lowering serum iron; inflammation raises hepcidin, producing anemia of chronic disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepcidin decreases, not increases, effective iron absorption by degrading ferroportin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythropoietin is regulated by tissue oxygenation, not by hepcidin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduction of ferric to ferrous iron is done by duodenal cytochrome b/ferrireductase, not hepcidin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepcidin does not act by increasing transferrin synthesis.

questions.stem: After dietary iron is reduced to the ferrous (Fe2+) state and absorbed across the enterocyte apical membrane via DMT1, then exported to the bloodstream through ferroportin, it must be carried through plasma to tissues such as the bone marrow. Which plasma protein transports iron in the blood?

explanation.summary: Transferrin carries iron in plasma to tissues.
explanation.whyCorrect: After export via ferroportin and oxidation to Fe3+, iron binds transferrin, the plasma transport protein that delivers iron to cells (e.g., erythroid precursors) via transferrin receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ferritin is the intracellular iron storage protein, not the plasma transporter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepcidin regulates iron efflux by degrading ferroportin; it does not transport iron.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Albumin carries unconjugated bilirubin and many drugs, but transferrin is the specific iron carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin, not plasma iron.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a hypercoagulable state is found to have an acute portal vein thrombosis on CT. Despite complete occlusion of the main portal vein, her AST and ALT remain near normal and she has no signs of hepatic failure. Which mechanism best explains why hepatocyte injury is minimal in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatocytes derive their oxygen predominantly from the portal vein

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced portal flow allows adenosine to accumulate, dilating the hepatic artery

choices.label: C
choices.text: The liver rapidly regenerates portal venous collaterals within hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: Portal blood carries no oxygen and is metabolically unimportant to hepatocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bile canalicular flow compensates for lost portal perfusion

explanation.summary: The hepatic arterial buffer response protects the liver when portal inflow falls.
explanation.whyCorrect: When portal flow decreases, less adenosine is washed out of the periportal space of Mall; the accumulating adenosine dilates the hepatic arteriole and increases arterial inflow to maintain total liver perfusion, limiting ischemic hepatocyte injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatocytes receive oxygen from both the portal vein and hepatic artery, and the arterial supply is well oxygenated; it is not portal-dominant for oxygen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Collateral formation (cavernous transformation) occurs over weeks in chronic PVT, not acutely, and does not explain immediate preservation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Portal blood does deliver oxygen and nutrients; the point is that the artery compensates, not that portal blood is unimportant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bile canalicular flow is a secretory pathway and does not supply oxygen or perfuse hepatocytes.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with polycythemia vera presents with abdominal pain, tender hepatomegaly, and new ascites. Contrast-enhanced CT shows patchy peripheral liver enhancement with thrombosis of the hepatic veins, and one region of the liver appears enlarged with preserved enhancement. Which anatomic structure accounts for that spared, hypertrophied region?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The left lateral segment, which drains via the falciform ligament

choices.label: B
choices.text: The quadrate lobe, which drains into the portal vein

choices.label: C
choices.text: The caudate lobe, which drains directly into the inferior vena cava

choices.label: D
choices.text: The right posterior segment, which drains into the middle hepatic vein

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gallbladder fossa, which is perfused by the cystic artery

explanation.summary: Budd-Chiari syndrome spares the caudate lobe because of its independent venous drainage.
explanation.whyCorrect: The caudate lobe drains directly into the IVC through small separate veins rather than through the main hepatic veins, so it is protected from hepatic vein thrombosis and often undergoes compensatory hypertrophy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The left lateral segment drains through the left hepatic vein and is not selectively spared; the falciform ligament is not a venous drainage route.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The quadrate lobe (segment IV) drains through hepatic veins, not the portal vein, and is not the spared lobe.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The right posterior segment drains via the right hepatic vein and is involved, not spared, in hepatic vein thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The gallbladder fossa is not a hepatic venous drainage territory and is unrelated to the sparing pattern.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with long-standing right-sided heart failure and tricuspid regurgitation has mild hepatomegaly and a slightly elevated alkaline phosphatase. A liver biopsy shows a mottled cut surface and centrilobular (zone 3) congestion with atrophic hepatocytes, while the periportal regions are relatively spared. Which term best describes this liver?

explanation.summary: Chronic passive venous congestion from right heart failure produces the classic nutmeg liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: Congestive hepatopathy results from chronic passive venous congestion (right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, tricuspid disease), producing centrilobular congestion and atrophy that spares periportal zones, creating the mottled 'nutmeg liver' appearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The florid duct lesion is the granulomatous small bile duct destruction of primary biliary cholangitis, not congestion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Onion-skin periductal fibrosis is characteristic of primary sclerosing cholangitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ground-glass hepatocytes suggest chronic hepatitis B (accumulated surface antigen), unrelated to congestion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Interface hepatitis is the hallmark of autoimmune hepatitis, an inflammatory rather than congestive process.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted with septic shock and prolonged hypotension. Two days later his AST is 3,400 U/L and ALT is 2,900 U/L, and his LDH is markedly elevated; bilirubin is only mildly increased. With restoration of blood pressure his transaminases fall rapidly over several days. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A rapid, massive transaminase spike after hypotension that resolves with reperfusion is ischemic hepatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Severe hepatic hypoperfusion during shock causes acute centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis, producing markedly elevated AST/ALT (often >1000) and high LDH; it is typically reversible once perfusion is restored.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune hepatitis produces a more gradual hepatocellular rise with elevated IgG and autoantibodies, not an abrupt shock-related spike that resolves with reperfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PBC is a chronic cholestatic disease with high alkaline phosphatase and AMA, not an acute transaminase spike.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ascending cholangitis causes a cholestatic pattern with fever and jaundice (Charcot triad), not isolated massive transaminitis that reverses with blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Amoxicillin-clavulanate injury is cholestatic/mixed with high alkaline phosphatase, not an acute hemodynamic hepatocellular necrosis.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with fatigue and elevated AST/ALT has a serum IgG well above normal and positive anti-smooth muscle antibodies. Liver biopsy shows a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate crossing the limiting plate into the parenchyma while sparing the bile ducts. Which histologic finding is being described?

explanation.summary: Interface hepatitis with plasma cells is the classic biopsy finding of autoimmune hepatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune hepatitis produces inflammation at the portal-parenchymal border (limiting plate) that spares bile ducts, with lymphocytes and plasma cells; combined with elevated IgG and anti-smooth muscle antibodies this is diagnostic.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulomatous bile duct destruction (florid duct lesion) points to primary biliary cholangitis, which targets ducts rather than sparing them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Centrilobular congestion reflects passive venous congestion (congestive hepatopathy), not an immune interface process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Onion-skin periductal fibrosis is the hallmark of primary sclerosing cholangitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microvesicular steatosis suggests toxic/metabolic injury (e.g., Reye syndrome, tetracycline), not autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman reports months of fatigue and pruritus. Labs show a cholestatic pattern with markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase, and testing is positive for anti-mitochondrial antibodies. The disease targets which structure?

explanation.summary: AMA-positive cholestatic disease in a middle-aged woman is primary biliary cholangitis, which destroys small intrahepatic ducts.
explanation.whyCorrect: PBC is an autoimmune destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts, marked by anti-mitochondrial antibodies (~90-95% sensitive) and a cholestatic (high alkaline phosphatase) pattern with pruritus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Attack on the hepatocyte limiting plate (interface hepatitis) describes autoimmune hepatitis, not PBC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Predominant large/extrahepatic duct strictures characterize primary sclerosing cholangitis, not PBC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatic venule involvement occurs in sinusoidal obstruction syndrome or congestion, not PBC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Portal vein radicle disease relates to portal vascular disorders, not the bile duct autoimmunity of PBC.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with ulcerative colitis is evaluated for an elevated alkaline phosphatase. MRCP shows multifocal strictures and dilations of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, giving a beaded appearance. Anti-mitochondrial antibody is negative. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Beaded intra- and extrahepatic strictures in a young man with IBD and negative AMA are diagnostic of PSC.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary sclerosing cholangitis causes multifocal strictures of intra- and extrahepatic ducts ('beaded' on MRCP), is strongly associated with ulcerative colitis (70-85%), and is AMA-negative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PBC is AMA-positive, affects small intrahepatic ducts in middle-aged women, and does not produce large-duct beading.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoimmune hepatitis is a hepatocellular disease with interface hepatitis, not a biliary stricturing disease on MRCP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A stone would produce a focal obstruction with upstream dilation, not diffuse multifocal beaded strictures.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Congestive hepatopathy is a venous congestion disorder without bile duct strictures.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old presents 30 hours after a large intentional acetaminophen ingestion with AST and ALT over 4,000 U/L. Biopsy would be expected to show necrosis concentrated in which hepatic region, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Zone 1 (periportal), because it receives the most oxygenated blood

choices.label: B
choices.text: Zone 2 (midzonal), because it is metabolically inactive

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bile ductular epithelium, because acetaminophen is concentrated in bile

choices.label: D
choices.text: Zone 3 (centrilobular), because cytochrome P450 activity is highest there

choices.label: E
choices.text: Portal tracts, because immune complexes deposit there

explanation.summary: Acetaminophen toxicity causes centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis where P450 generates NAPQI.
explanation.whyCorrect: In overdose, conjugation pathways are saturated and more drug is shunted through cytochrome P450 to the toxic metabolite NAPQI; because P450 (CYP2E1) activity is highest in zone 3, NAPQI accumulates there once glutathione is depleted, causing centrilobular necrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Zone 1 is best oxygenated and has lower P450 activity, so it is relatively resistant to NAPQI-mediated necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Zone 2 is not metabolically inactive and is not the primary site of acetaminophen necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acetaminophen injury is hepatocellular in zone 3, not a bile ductular process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Portal tract immune-complex deposition is not the mechanism of acetaminophen toxicity.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old is treated for a toxic acetaminophen level using N-acetylcysteine. By what primary mechanism does this antidote reduce hepatic injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds acetaminophen directly in the gut to block absorption

choices.label: B
choices.text: It inhibits cytochrome P450 to prevent NAPQI formation

choices.label: C
choices.text: It competitively displaces NAPQI from DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: It chelates iron to reduce oxidative stress

choices.label: E
choices.text: It replenishes glutathione by providing cysteine

explanation.summary: N-acetylcysteine works chiefly by restoring glutathione stores.
explanation.whyCorrect: NAC provides cysteine, the rate-limiting substrate for glutathione synthesis; replenished glutathione conjugates and detoxifies the reactive metabolite NAPQI, limiting centrilobular necrosis. It is most effective when given within 8 hours of ingestion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activated charcoal, not NAC, adsorbs acetaminophen in the gut; NAC acts systemically by supporting glutathione.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NAC does not primarily act by inhibiting P450; its main role is glutathione repletion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NAPQI toxicity is via protein adduct formation and oxidative injury, and NAC does not displace it from DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron chelation (e.g., deferoxamine) is unrelated to acetaminophen detoxification.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with latent tuberculosis started therapy six weeks ago. He uses alcohol regularly and is a slow acetylator. He now has nausea, jaundice, and a hepatocellular transaminase elevation. Which drug most likely caused this idiosyncratic injury?

explanation.summary: Isoniazid is a classic cause of idiosyncratic hepatocellular DILI, especially with alcohol use and older age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Isoniazid causes idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury via reactive acetylated metabolites; risk rises with older age, alcohol use, and (per classic teaching) acetylator status, matching this TB patient's presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Amoxicillin-clavulanate causes a cholestatic/mixed pattern, not the hepatocellular injury described, and is not part of TB therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ursodeoxycholic acid is used to treat cholestatic disease and is not a typical hepatotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: N-acetylcysteine is a hepatoprotective antidote, not a cause of hepatocellular injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carbon tetrachloride is an industrial solvent, not a prescribed antituberculosis drug in this scenario.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman develops jaundice and pruritus three weeks after completing a course of an antibiotic for sinusitis. Labs show a markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase with only mildly elevated transaminases (a cholestatic pattern). Which agent is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is a leading cause of cholestatic/mixed idiosyncratic DILI.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amoxicillin-clavulanate causes idiosyncratic cholestatic or mixed liver injury, attributed to clavulanate-related immune-mediated bile duct injury, and characteristically presents weeks after exposure with a cholestatic (high alkaline phosphatase) pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetaminophen produces acute hepatocellular necrosis with very high transaminases, not a delayed cholestatic pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbon tetrachloride causes centrilobular hepatocellular necrosis via free radicals, not cholestasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isoniazid injury is hepatocellular, not predominantly cholestatic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-amanitin causes fulminant hepatocellular failure, not an isolated cholestatic pattern after an antibiotic.

questions.stem: A factory worker is exposed to a chlorinated industrial solvent and develops centrilobular hepatocellular necrosis. The toxin is metabolized by CYP2E1 into a trichloromethyl free radical that initiates membrane lipid peroxidation. Which agent is responsible?

explanation.summary: Carbon tetrachloride is the classic model of free-radical, lipid-peroxidation hepatotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbon tetrachloride is metabolized by CYP2E1 into a trichloromethyl free radical that triggers membrane lipid peroxidation and centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis, the classic experimental model of free-radical hepatotoxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Isoniazid causes idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury via reactive acetylated metabolites, not free-radical lipid peroxidation from a solvent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acetaminophen injury is mediated by NAPQI and glutathione depletion, not by a trichloromethyl radical, and it is a drug rather than an industrial solvent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Amoxicillin-clavulanate causes immune-mediated cholestatic injury, not free-radical necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ursodeoxycholic acid is a therapeutic bile acid, not a hepatotoxic solvent.

questions.stem: A family becomes ill 8 hours after foraging and eating wild mushrooms, with vomiting and watery diarrhea, then transiently improves before developing acute liver failure with coagulopathy on day 5. The responsible toxin causes hepatocyte death by which mechanism?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune-mediated destruction of small bile ducts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of RNA polymerase II, halting mRNA and protein synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation blockade causing microvesicular steatosis

explanation.summary: Amanita phalloides (alpha-amanitin) kills hepatocytes by inhibiting RNA polymerase II.
explanation.whyCorrect: The delayed GI phase (6-12 h), false-recovery window, and fulminant failure on days 4-7 are classic for Amanita phalloides; its toxin alpha-amanitin inhibits RNA polymerase II, halting mRNA/protein synthesis and causing hepatocyte death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glutathione depletion is the mechanism of acetaminophen toxicity, not amatoxin poisoning.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Trichloromethyl free radicals mediate carbon tetrachloride injury, not mushroom toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune destruction of small bile ducts describes primary biliary cholangitis, not an acute toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microvesicular steatosis from impaired fatty acid oxidation characterizes agents like tetracycline or Reye syndrome, not alpha-amanitin.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl has autoimmune hepatitis. Serologic testing is negative for anti-smooth muscle antibody and ANA but is positive for a different autoantibody that defines the type-2 subtype of the disease. Which antibody is it?

explanation.summary: Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis is defined by anti-LKM1 antibodies, often in children.
explanation.whyCorrect: AIH type 1 is defined by ANA and/or anti-smooth muscle antibodies, whereas type 2, more common in children, is defined by anti-liver-kidney microsomal type 1 (anti-LKM1) antibodies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-mitochondrial antibody is the marker of primary biliary cholangitis, not AIH type 2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited systemic sclerosis (CREST), not AIH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p-ANCA can be seen in PSC and some AIH but does not define the type-2 subtype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-dsDNA is specific for systemic lupus erythematosus, not AIH type 2.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with primary biliary cholangitis based on cholestatic labs and positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies. Which first-line therapy improves bile flow and slows disease progression?

explanation.summary: Ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line therapy for PBC.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ursodeoxycholic acid improves bile flow and slows histologic and biochemical progression of PBC, making it the standard first-line treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Corticosteroids are first-line for autoimmune hepatitis, not PBC, and are not the standard PBC therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: N-acetylcysteine treats acetaminophen toxicity, not PBC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transplantation is reserved for advanced/refractory disease, not initial therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anticoagulation treats thrombotic vascular disorders such as Budd-Chiari, not an autoimmune cholestatic disease.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with an underlying myeloproliferative disorder is diagnosed with symptomatic Budd-Chiari syndrome and started on anticoagulation, but he continues to have refractory ascites and progressive congestion despite adequate anticoagulation. Which is the most appropriate next step in the escalation of management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Observation, since Budd-Chiari often resolves spontaneously

choices.label: B
choices.text: Angioplasty/stenting or a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid to improve bile flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: High-dose corticosteroids to suppress hepatic inflammation

explanation.summary: When anticoagulation fails in Budd-Chiari, escalate to angioplasty/stenting or TIPS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Budd-Chiari management escalates stepwise: lifelong anticoagulation and treating the prothrombotic disorder first, then angioplasty/stenting of the obstructed vein or TIPS for decompression, and finally transplantation for refractory disease. With refractory congestion despite anticoagulation, endovascular decompression (angioplasty/stenting or TIPS) is the next step.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Budd-Chiari is always treated; observation is inappropriate because obstruction causes progressive congestion and fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ursodeoxycholic acid treats cholestatic autoimmune disease and has no role in venous outflow obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Corticosteroids treat autoimmune hepatitis, not the mechanical/thrombotic obstruction of Budd-Chiari.
whyWrongByChoice.E: N-acetylcysteine is an antidote for acetaminophen toxicity, not a treatment for hepatic venous outflow obstruction.

questions.stem: A hepatologist notes that among patients presenting with portal vein thrombosis, one underlying condition is identified far more often than any other. Which is the single most common cause of portal vein thrombosis?

explanation.summary: Cirrhosis is the most common cause of portal vein thrombosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cirrhosis produces venous stasis and a prothrombotic shift in the portal system, making it the most common cause of portal vein thrombosis (fitting Virchow's triad of stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oral contraceptives contribute to hypercoagulability and can precipitate PVT but are not the single most common cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Right-sided heart failure causes congestive hepatopathy (venous outflow congestion), not portal vein thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Constrictive pericarditis causes passive hepatic congestion, not portal vein thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tricuspid regurgitation causes congestive hepatopathy, not portal inflow thrombosis.

questions.stem: A hematologist is asked which single risk factor is shared by both portal vein thrombosis and Budd-Chiari syndrome, since the two disorders otherwise have distinct causes. Which factor is common to both?

explanation.summary: Hypercoagulability, especially myeloproliferative disorders, underlies both PVT and Budd-Chiari.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both portal vein thrombosis and Budd-Chiari syndrome share hypercoagulable states, particularly myeloproliferative disorders (e.g., polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia), as a common risk factor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Right heart failure causes congestive hepatopathy, not both thrombotic disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cirrhosis is a major cause of PVT but not of Budd-Chiari, so it is not shared.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intra-abdominal inflammation is a cause of PVT (local venous injury) but not of hepatic vein thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Constrictive pericarditis causes passive congestion, not shared thrombotic risk for both disorders.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents 6 hours after a single acute acetaminophen overdose. She is asymptomatic with normal transaminases. Which is the most appropriate tool to decide whether to start N-acetylcysteine?

choices.label: D
choices.text: King's College criteria for immediate transplantation

explanation.summary: The Rumack-Matthew nomogram guides NAC treatment after a single acute acetaminophen ingestion.
explanation.whyCorrect: For a single acute ingestion, plotting the serum acetaminophen level against time since ingestion on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram (treatment line ~150 mcg/mL at 4 hours) determines whether NAC is indicated; it is most accurate 4-24 hours post-ingestion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Child-Pugh score grades chronic liver disease severity, not acute acetaminophen risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MELD predicts mortality/transplant priority in chronic liver disease, not acute overdose treatment thresholds.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ranson criteria assess acute pancreatitis severity, unrelated to acetaminophen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: King's College criteria identify acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure needing transplant, not the initial decision to start NAC after a fresh single ingestion.

questions.stem: A student asks why the liver tolerates a period of systemic hypotension far better than the kidney, which readily develops acute tubular necrosis in shock. Which explanation is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The liver has a dual blood supply and the hepatic arterial buffer response

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatocytes have no metabolic oxygen demand

choices.label: D
choices.text: The liver is perfused entirely by the portal vein, which is unaffected by systemic pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: The liver receives preferential sympathetic vasodilation during shock

explanation.summary: The liver's dual supply and hepatic arterial buffer response make it relatively tolerant of hypoperfusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The liver receives blood from both the portal vein and hepatic artery, and the hepatic arterial buffer response increases arterial inflow when portal flow falls; together these buffer perfusion, whereas the highly perfusion-dependent kidney develops acute tubular necrosis. Only severe/prolonged hypoperfusion overcomes this to cause ischemic hepatitis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatocytes are metabolically active and do have significant oxygen demand.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatocytes do not store meaningful intracellular oxygen reserves.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The liver is not perfused solely by the portal vein; it has a dual supply, and portal pressure does fall in shock.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no preferential sympathetic vasodilation of the liver during shock; the protection comes from dual supply and the buffer response.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with obesity and type 2 diabetes is found to have mildly elevated aminotransferases on routine labs. An ultrasound shows increased hepatic echogenicity, and he denies alcohol use. He is told his condition, previously called nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), now has an updated name that reflects its underlying cause. Which term best describes his condition?

explanation.summary: NAFLD was renamed MASLD to emphasize its metabolic etiology.
explanation.whyCorrect: MASLD is the current term for what was formerly called NAFLD, describing fatty liver disease driven by metabolic dysfunction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alcohol-associated liver disease is excluded by the absence of significant alcohol use.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary biliary cholangitis produces a cholestatic pattern with elevated alkaline phosphatase, not steatosis on ultrasound.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autoimmune hepatitis is not the renamed form of NAFLD and involves autoantibodies and interface hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemochromatosis reflects iron overload, not the metabolic-driven steatosis described here.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with obesity, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes is diagnosed with MASLD. Her physician explains that a single metabolic mechanism is the most widely supported driver linking her conditions to hepatic fat accumulation and inflammation. Which mechanism is this?

explanation.summary: Insulin resistance is the central, most widely supported driver of MASLD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin resistance links hepatic steatosis and steatohepatitis to obesity and type 2 diabetes and is the most widely supported mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Viral hepatitis is a distinct cause of liver injury, not the metabolic driver of MASLD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autoimmune bile duct destruction describes primary biliary cholangitis, not MASLD pathogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Copper accumulation describes Wilson disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited protein misfolding disorder, not the driver of MASLD.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is being evaluated for suspected MASLD. His labs show AST 40 U/L and ALT 55 U/L. He drinks no alcohol. Which interpretation of his AST-to-ALT ratio best supports a diagnosis of MASLD rather than alcohol-associated liver injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A ratio greater than 2 favors MASLD

choices.label: B
choices.text: A ratio equal to exactly 1.0 is diagnostic of alcohol injury

choices.label: C
choices.text: A ratio less than 1 favors MASLD

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ratio cannot distinguish the two conditions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only bilirubin, not the ratio, distinguishes them

explanation.summary: An AST/ALT ratio below 1 favors MASLD; above 2 favors alcohol injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: His ratio is about 0.7 (less than 1), which is characteristic of non-alcohol-related (MASLD) hepatic injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A ratio greater than 2 suggests alcohol-related injury, not MASLD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A ratio of 1.0 is not specifically diagnostic of alcohol injury; alcohol classically gives greater than 2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ratio does provide useful discrimination between MASLD and alcoholic injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bilirubin is not the distinguishing feature; the AST-to-ALT ratio is the relevant marker here.

questions.stem: A liver biopsy from a patient with progressive MASLD shows fat accumulation plus lobular inflammation, ballooned hepatocytes, and eosinophilic rope-like intracellular inclusions. Which stage of the MASLD spectrum does this histology represent?

explanation.summary: Inflammation, ballooning, and Mallory bodies define MASH.
explanation.whyCorrect: MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) adds inflammation, ballooned hepatocytes, and Mallory-Denk bodies to the fat accumulation of steatosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Simple steatosis shows fat droplets alone without inflammation, ballooning, or Mallory bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A normal liver would lack the steatosis and inflammatory features described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cirrhosis is defined by significant fibrosis and regenerative nodules, which are not described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HCC is a malignant tumor, not the inflammatory steatohepatitis picture described.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with newly diagnosed MASLD and metabolic syndrome asks what she can do to prevent her disease from progressing. She takes metformin for diabetes. What is the most appropriate first-line intervention?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Weight loss and increased physical activity

explanation.summary: Lifestyle change targeting metabolic syndrome is first-line for MASLD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment centers on the underlying metabolic syndrome through weight loss, exercise, and diabetes control, which can lower aminotransferases and slow progression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transplantation is reserved for end-stage disease, not initial MASLD management.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corticosteroids are not a mainstay of MASLD treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Statins are generally continued in MASLD; stopping them is not indicated and does not treat the disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antivirals treat viral hepatitis, not metabolic-driven MASLD.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is evaluated for possible MASLD. His physician wants to confirm the strongest, most well-supported risk factor cluster associated with the disease. Which of the following best fits this description?

choices.label: C
choices.text: A family history of autoimmune disease

explanation.summary: Metabolic syndrome is the strongest risk factor for MASLD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metabolic syndrome, a cluster of abdominal obesity, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, and hypertension, is the most well-supported risk factor for MASLD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Recent viral illness is not the established risk factor cluster for MASLD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autoimmune disease family history is unrelated to the metabolic-driven MASLD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acetaminophen use causes dose-dependent hepatotoxicity, not the chronic metabolic steatosis of MASLD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusion history relates to viral hepatitis risk, not MASLD.

questions.stem: A researcher studying MASLD focuses on an adipose-derived hormone that increases insulin sensitivity and has anti-inflammatory effects. She notes that its level changes as a patient gains fat mass. How does this hormone behave as adiposity increases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adiponectin levels rise proportionally with fat mass

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adiponectin levels fall as fat mass rises

explanation.summary: Adiponectin is inversely correlated with body weight.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adiponectin decreases as adipose tissue increases, reducing insulin sensitivity and promoting MASLD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adiponectin is inversely, not directly, correlated with fat mass.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The hormone in question is adiponectin, and it does not become undetectable; leptin actually rises with adiposity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adiponectin does change—it falls with rising fat mass.
