explanation.whyCorrect: Wilson disease typically presents before age 40 (often in childhood/adolescence) and uniquely combines hepatic dysfunction with neuropsychiatric features such as tremor and behavioral change from copper deposition in the brain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemochromatosis presents in middle age with iron overload, not adolescent neuropsychiatric disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes liver and lung disease, not the tremor/behavioral neuropsychiatric picture of copper deposition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gilbert syndrome causes benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia without hepatitis or neurologic signs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary sclerosing cholangitis causes cholestatic bile-duct disease, not this neuropsychiatric presentation.

questions.topicName: Inherited Metabolic Liver Diseases (Wilson, Hemochromatosis, A1AT)
questions.stem: In hereditary hemochromatosis, HFE loss-of-function leads to systemic iron overload. Which best describes the role of hepcidin in this process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepcidin normally acts as the 'brakes' on iron absorption, and its reduced activity releases those brakes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepcidin normally increases intestinal iron uptake, and its excess drives overload

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepcidin is the main iron storage protein whose loss frees stored iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepcidin carries iron in the plasma, and its saturation raises transferrin saturation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hepcidin chelates dietary iron in the gut lumen to prevent absorption

explanation.summary: Hepcidin restrains iron absorption; its dysfunction releases the brakes and causes overload.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepcidin is the hormonal 'brake' limiting dietary iron absorption; disordered/reduced hepcidin (from HFE dysfunction) allows unregulated iron entry into the portal circulation and accumulation in tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepcidin restrains rather than increases iron uptake; overload results from too little effective hepcidin, not excess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ferritin, not hepcidin, is the main iron storage protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transferrin, not hepcidin, carries iron in plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepcidin regulates absorption via ferroportin, not by directly chelating luminal iron.

questions.topicName: Inherited Metabolic Liver Diseases (Wilson, Hemochromatosis, A1AT)
questions.stem: A screening program for hereditary hemochromatosis wants the single most useful blood marker to flag iron overload before confirmatory testing. Which marker is most important, and what threshold is considered specific?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Serum ferritin above 200 ng/mL in all adults

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transferrin saturation above roughly 60% in men or 50% in women

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum hepcidin above the upper reference limit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unbound serum copper above the reference range

explanation.summary: Transferrin saturation is the most important hemochromatosis marker, specific above ~60% (men)/50% (women).
explanation.whyCorrect: Transferrin saturation is the key screening marker for hemochromatosis, with good specificity when above approximately 60% in men or 50% in women, prompting confirmatory ferritin and genetic testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and, while supportive, is less specific as the primary screening marker than transferrin saturation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TIBC is low, not high, in iron overload, so a high threshold points the wrong direction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepcidin is inappropriately low/dysfunctional in HFE hemochromatosis and is not the standard screening marker.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum copper is a Wilson disease parameter, irrelevant to screening for iron overload.

questions.topicName: Inherited Metabolic Liver Diseases (Wilson, Hemochromatosis, A1AT)
questions.stem: A patient with iron overload also has significant anemia and cannot tolerate blood removal. Which approach to reducing iron burden is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aggressive weekly phlebotomy regardless of hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Zinc supplementation to block iron absorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron chelation therapy (e.g., deferoxamine) instead of phlebotomy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Withholding all treatment until anemia resolves spontaneously

explanation.summary: Anemic iron-overload patients need chelation, since they cannot tolerate phlebotomy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients who are anemic cannot spare the red cell loss of phlebotomy, so iron is removed with chelating drugs such as deferoxamine instead.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aggressive phlebotomy would worsen anemia; it is contraindicated when the patient cannot spare red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Zinc induces metallothionein to limit copper (Wilson disease) absorption, not to remove iron.
whyWrongByChoice.D: D-penicillamine chelates copper, not iron, and is not the treatment for iron overload.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Untreated iron overload progresses to organ damage; deferral is inappropriate when effective chelation exists.

questions.topicName: Inherited Metabolic Liver Diseases (Wilson, Hemochromatosis, A1AT)
questions.stem: A 46-year-old with PiZZ alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency has decompensated cirrhosis and also early emphysema. He undergoes liver transplantation. What is the expected effect on his disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transplant cures both the hepatic and the pulmonary disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transplant worsens the emphysema by increasing circulating mutant A1AT

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transplant has no effect on the liver disease but halts the emphysema

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transplant is curative for the hepatic disease but does not alter the course of the pulmonary disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transplant restores normal A1AT genotype in all body tissues

explanation.summary: Liver transplant cures the hepatic disease of A1AT deficiency but not the lung disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The donor liver produces normal alpha-1 antitrypsin and eliminates hepatic protein accumulation, curing the liver disease; however, pre-existing pulmonary damage is not reversed and the emphysema course is unchanged.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transplant does not cure the pulmonary disease; established emphysema persists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The transplanted liver makes normal A1AT and does not increase mutant protein or worsen the lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is reversed: transplant addresses the liver disease, not established lung damage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transplant changes only the liver's genotype (the graft); the recipient's other tissues retain PiZZ.

questions.topicName: Inherited Metabolic Liver Diseases (Wilson, Hemochromatosis, A1AT)
questions.stem: A patient with Wilson disease develops nephrotoxicity and a lupus-like immunologic reaction on D-penicillamine, requiring a switch. Which agent is the most appropriate alternative copper chelator with comparable efficacy and fewer adverse effects?

explanation.summary: Trientine is the standard alternative copper chelator to D-penicillamine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trientine was developed as an alternative to D-penicillamine and offers comparable copper-chelating efficacy with fewer adverse effects, making it the appropriate switch when penicillamine is not tolerated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deferoxamine chelates iron for hemochromatosis, not copper for Wilson disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Deferasirox is an oral iron chelator used in iron overload, not a copper chelator.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dimercaprol is a parenteral heavy-metal chelator, not the standard maintenance alternative to penicillamine in Wilson disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcium disodium EDTA is used chiefly for lead poisoning, not as the preferred copper chelator in Wilson disease.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a long history of alcohol use presents with abdominal distention, jaundice, and lower-extremity edema. Liver biopsy shows bridging bands of collagen surrounding islands of hepatocytes, with disrupted lobular architecture. Which cell type is primarily responsible for producing the collagen seen on this biopsy?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatic stellate cells in the space of Disse

explanation.summary: Fibrosis in cirrhosis is driven by activated hepatic stellate cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: With chronic injury, hepatic stellate cells in the space of Disse transform into myofibroblasts that secrete collagen, producing the bridging fibrosis of cirrhosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Kupffer cells are resident hepatic macrophages that release cytokines but do not themselves lay down the collagen matrix.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Regenerative nodules are clusters of surviving hepatocytes trapped by fibrous bands; they do not produce collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sinusoidal endothelial cells line the sinusoids and undergo capillarization but are not the principal collagen source.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cholangiocytes line bile ducts and proliferate in cholestatic disease but are not the myofibroblast precursor driving fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with cirrhosis develops massive hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals actively bleeding dilated veins in the distal esophagus. These varices form because of anastomoses between the portal circulation and which venous system?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Superior rectal vein and middle/inferior rectal veins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Paraumbilical veins and superficial epigastric veins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Splenic vein and left renal vein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Left gastric vein and azygos/esophageal veins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Superior mesenteric vein and inferior mesenteric vein

explanation.summary: Esophageal varices arise from the left gastric-to-esophageal (azygos) portosystemic anastomosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Portal hypertension diverts blood from the left gastric vein into esophageal veins that drain into the azygos (systemic) system, producing esophageal varices prone to rupture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The superior-to-inferior rectal anastomosis produces anorectal varices, not esophageal varices.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Paraumbilical-to-epigastric anastomoses produce caput medusae around the umbilicus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spleen-to-renal shunting relates to spontaneous splenorenal shunts, not esophageal varices.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both mesenteric veins are part of the portal system; connecting them does not create a portosystemic shunt.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with new-onset ascites undergoes diagnostic paracentesis. His serum albumin is 3.0 g/dL and his ascitic fluid albumin is 1.5 g/dL. Which of the following does this gradient most strongly indicate?

explanation.summary: A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or greater indicates portal hypertension.
explanation.whyCorrect: The serum-to-ascites albumin gradient is 3.0 minus 1.5 equals 1.5 g/dL. A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or greater indicates portal hypertension as the cause of ascites.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Peritoneal carcinomatosis produces a low SAAG (<1.1), reflecting a non-portal hypertensive exudative process.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tuberculous peritonitis also gives a low SAAG from protein-rich exudate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nephrotic syndrome causes a low SAAG because hypoalbuminemia rather than portal pressure drives the ascites.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancreatic ascites is a low-SAAG, high-amylase exudate, not a portal hypertensive fluid.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites presents with fever, abdominal pain, and worsening confusion. Paracentesis is performed. Which ascitic fluid finding confirms spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?

explanation.summary: SBP is defined by an ascitic neutrophil count above 250/mm3.
explanation.whyCorrect: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed when ascitic fluid shows more than 250 neutrophils/mm3, most often due to gut organisms such as E. coli and Klebsiella.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A low SAAG points away from portal hypertensive ascites and does not diagnose infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Elevated ascitic amylase suggests pancreatic ascites, not SBP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A high ascitic glucose is not a criterion; SBP is defined by the neutrophil count.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A high total protein suggests secondary peritonitis or cardiac ascites, not the neutrophil threshold that defines SBP.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with cirrhosis becomes increasingly drowsy and confused. On exam, when asked to extend her arms and dorsiflex her wrists, her hands flap downward intermittently. Which mechanism best explains her neurological state?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Accumulation of ammonia and other toxins

explanation.summary: Hepatic encephalopathy with asterixis results from impaired hepatic detoxification of ammonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The failing liver cannot clear ammonia and other nitrogenous toxins; astrocytes convert excess ammonia and glutamate to glutamine, driving encephalopathy, and asterixis reflects the resulting loss of muscle tone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reduced clotting factor synthesis raises the INR and causes bleeding, not confusion and asterixis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Low albumin contributes to ascites and edema, not directly to encephalopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelet sequestration causes thrombocytopenia, not the neurologic picture described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary shunting (hepatopulmonary syndrome) causes hypoxemia and dyspnea, not asterixis; the flapping tremor is ammonia-driven.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with cirrhosis is admitted with confusion. His nurse begins a medication that acidifies the colonic lumen. Which of the following best describes how this drug lowers serum ammonia?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It acidifies the gut lumen, converting ammonia (NH3) to ammonium (NH4+)

choices.label: C
choices.text: It enhances renal excretion of ammonium in the urine

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stimulates hepatocyte regeneration to restore urea cycle function

choices.label: E
choices.text: It binds ammonia in the bloodstream to form a soluble complex

explanation.summary: Lactulose acidifies the colon, trapping ammonia as ammonium for fecal excretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lactulose is metabolized by colonic bacteria to acids that lower luminal pH, converting NH3 to poorly absorbed NH4+, which is trapped in the lumen and eliminated in stool.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactulose does not act on hepatic glutaminase; it works in the gut lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Its effect is fecal trapping of ammonium, not enhanced renal excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: It does not restore hepatocyte function or the urea cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It does not bind ammonia in the blood; it acts locally in the colon.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with rapidly rising serum creatinine (from 0.9 to 2.8 mg/dL over a week). Urinalysis is bland, urine sodium is 6 mEq/L, there is no proteinuria, and renal ultrasound shows no obstruction. He has not improved with volume expansion. Which statement about his condition is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The kidneys have intrinsic structural damage that will persist after liver transplant

choices.label: B
choices.text: It results from reflex renal vasoconstriction

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is best treated with high-dose loop diuretics to increase urine output

choices.label: D
choices.text: A high urine sodium above 40 mEq/L is expected

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prompt response to a saline challenge confirms the diagnosis

explanation.summary: Hepatorenal syndrome is functional renal failure that reverses with liver transplant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatorenal syndrome is a pre-renal AKI from reflex renal vasoconstriction in severe cirrhosis; the kidneys are structurally normal, and renal function improves dramatically after liver transplantation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no intrinsic renal disease; recovery after transplant proves the kidneys are structurally intact.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aggressive diuresis worsens intravascular depletion and renal perfusion; it is not the treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urine sodium is characteristically very low (less than 10 mEq/L), reflecting avid sodium retention.
whyWrongByChoice.E: By definition HRS does not respond to volume expansion, distinguishing it from simple prerenal azotemia.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with cirrhosis reports shortness of breath that worsens when he sits up and improves when he lies down. Pulse oximetry shows lower oxygen saturation when upright than when supine. Which mechanism underlies this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pulmonary arterial vasoconstriction and elevated pulmonary pressures

choices.label: C
choices.text: Left heart failure from cirrhotic cardiomyopathy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intrapulmonary vascular dilation causing arteriovenous shunting

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recurrent pulmonary emboli from portal vein thrombosis

explanation.summary: Hepatopulmonary syndrome causes hypoxemia and orthodeoxia from intrapulmonary vascular dilation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatopulmonary syndrome features dilated pulmonary vessels that create arteriovenous shunts; upright posture worsens shunting through dilated basal vessels, producing platypnea and orthodeoxia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Portopulmonary hypertension involves vasoconstriction and high pulmonary pressures, the opposite of the vascular dilation causing orthodeoxia here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ascites-related dyspnea would not cause the characteristic worsening of hypoxemia specifically when upright.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy causes heart failure but not the position-dependent shunt physiology described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulmonary emboli cause acute dyspnea and hypoxemia but not the reproducible orthodeoxia of intrapulmonary dilation.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with cirrhosis has a platelet count of 70,000/mm3 without evidence of active bleeding or marrow disease. Her spleen is enlarged on exam. What is the most likely mechanism of her thrombocytopenia?

explanation.summary: Portal hypertension causes congestive splenomegaly, which sequesters platelets.
explanation.whyCorrect: Portal hypertension leads to congestive splenomegaly; the enlarged spleen sequesters circulating platelets, producing thrombocytopenia in cirrhosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no evidence of an autoimmune process; the mechanism is mechanical sequestration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelets are produced by bone marrow megakaryocytes, not synthesized by the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DIC would be accompanied by consumption of fibrinogen and schistocytes; the picture here is isolated splenic sequestration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperammonemia causes encephalopathy, not marrow suppression or thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with cirrhosis is being evaluated for liver transplantation. Which combination of laboratory values is used to calculate his MELD score and prioritize him on the transplant list?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Albumin, AST, ALT, and platelet count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ferritin, ceruloplasmin, GGT, and alkaline phosphatase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bilirubin, ascites, encephalopathy, and prothrombin time

explanation.summary: MELD uses bilirubin, creatinine, INR, and sodium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score is calculated from serum bilirubin, serum creatinine, INR, and serum sodium to stratify severity and allocate transplants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These are not MELD components; AST/ALT and platelets are used in other fibrosis indices.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ammonia and electrolytes other than sodium are not part of MELD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These are markers for specific etiologies (hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, cholestasis), not MELD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ascites and encephalopathy are subjective Child-Pugh components; MELD deliberately uses only objective labs.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with cirrhosis and moderate ascites remains fluid-overloaded despite dietary sodium restriction. Which pharmacologic regimen is the standard first-line diuretic therapy?

explanation.summary: First-line diuretic therapy for cirrhotic ascites pairs spironolactone with furosemide.
explanation.whyCorrect: When ascites persists despite sodium restriction, combining spironolactone (which counters the secondary hyperaldosteronism of cirrhosis) with furosemide provides effective, balanced natriuresis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Thiazides are weak in the setting of avid proximal sodium retention and are not standard.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acetazolamide is not used for cirrhotic ascites and risks metabolic acidosis worsening encephalopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic for cerebral edema, not ascites management.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Furosemide alone is less effective and promotes hypokalemia; spironolactone is the anchor drug given hyperaldosteronism.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with brisk hematemesis. After resuscitation, which medication should be started early to reduce splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure before endoscopy?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Propranolol given intravenously as a bolus

explanation.summary: Octreotide reduces splanchnic flow and portal pressure in acute variceal bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Octreotide, a somatostatin analog, causes splanchnic vasoconstriction that lowers portal blood flow and pressure, helping control variceal hemorrhage while endoscopy is arranged.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactulose treats encephalopathy and does not stop acute bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rifaximin is a gut antibiotic for encephalopathy, not acute hemostasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spironolactone manages ascites and has no role in acute bleeding control.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nonselective beta-blockers are for primary/secondary prophylaxis, not acute IV bolus therapy during active hemorrhage where octreotide is preferred.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with cirrhosis and recurrent variceal bleeding refractory to repeated endoscopic band ligation undergoes placement of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS). Two weeks later he develops worsening confusion and asterixis. Which complication of the procedure best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shunt thrombosis raising portal pressure further

choices.text: Diversion of portal blood past the liver, allowing ammonia to reach the systemic circulation

explanation.summary: TIPS worsens encephalopathy by shunting portal blood past hepatic detoxification.
explanation.whyCorrect: A TIPS connects the portal and hepatic veins so blood bypasses the liver; unmetabolized ammonia enters the systemic circulation, precipitating or worsening hepatic encephalopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Shunt thrombosis would cause recurrent bleeding or ascites, not new encephalopathy; a patent shunt is what allows the ammonia bypass.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TIPS connects venous structures and does not typically injure the hepatic artery to cause ischemic hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clinically significant hemolysis is not the mechanism of post-TIPS confusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TIPS reduces portal pressure and improves ascites; it does not typically worsen it to cause compartment syndrome.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with newly diagnosed cirrhosis has an INR of 1.8. His hepatologist explains that the liver produces both procoagulant and anticoagulant factors. Which set of vitamin K-dependent factors is most reduced in his liver failure?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factors II, VII, IX, X, protein C, and protein S

explanation.summary: Vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S fall in liver failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: The liver synthesizes the vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X plus the inhibitors protein C and protein S; their decline raises the INR, though loss of anticoagulants blunts a simple bleeding tendency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factors V and VIII are not vitamin K-dependent; factor VIII is often preserved or elevated in liver disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrinogen and vWF are affected but are not the vitamin K-dependent group asked about.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Factors XIII and XI are not the vitamin K-dependent factors reflected by the INR.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Factor VIII is not vitamin K-dependent, and tissue factor is not a hepatic clotting factor.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with cirrhosis has spider angiomas on his chest, reddened palms, and gynecomastia. Which underlying hormonal derangement best accounts for all three findings?

explanation.summary: Impaired hepatic estrogen clearance raises estrogen, causing spider angiomas, palmar erythema, and gynecomastia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cirrhotic liver fails to clear estrogen; the resulting hyperestrogenemia dilates cutaneous vessels (spider angiomas, palmar erythema) and causes gynecomastia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ammonia drives encephalopathy, not these estrogen-mediated cutaneous and breast findings.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Excess aldosterone promotes sodium and fluid retention, not spider angiomas or gynecomastia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: High cortisol produces Cushingoid features, not this triad.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Growth hormone excess causes acromegaly, not these estrogen-related signs.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis and known medium esophageal varices that have never bled is started on a medication for primary prophylaxis against variceal hemorrhage. A nonselective beta-blocker such as propranolol lowers portal pressure primarily through which combined effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduced cardiac output plus splanchnic vasoconstriction from unopposed alpha-1 activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Selective beta-1 blockade increasing renal sodium excretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct dilation of the intrahepatic sinusoids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alpha-1 receptor agonism causing systemic vasodilation

explanation.summary: Nonselective beta-blockers cut portal inflow via beta-1 and beta-2 blockade.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beta-1 blockade lowers cardiac output and splanchnic inflow, while beta-2 blockade leaves alpha-1-mediated splanchnic vasoconstriction unopposed; together they reduce portal blood flow and pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The benefit is hemodynamic reduction of portal inflow, not natriuresis, and nonselective (not selective beta-1) agents are used.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They act on systemic and splanchnic vessels and cardiac output, not by dilating intrahepatic sinusoids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: They do not act as alpha-1 agonists; unopposed endogenous alpha-1 tone is what constricts the splanchnic bed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Their portal effect is not through RAAS inhibition.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with dilated, tortuous subcutaneous veins radiating outward from her umbilicus. This finding results from recanalization and engorgement of which vessels?

explanation.summary: Caput medusae arises from paraumbilical-to-epigastric vein anastomoses.
explanation.whyCorrect: In portal hypertension, blood is shunted through recanalized paraumbilical veins into the systemic superficial epigastric veins, producing the tortuous periumbilical veins called caput medusae.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inferior mesenteric tributaries are part of the portal system draining the hindgut, not the periumbilical shunt.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Left gastric vein shunting produces esophageal varices, not caput medusae.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Superior rectal vein anastomoses produce anorectal varices.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic vein collaterals relate to splenomegaly and splenorenal shunts, not the umbilical pattern.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man with a 20-year history of heavy alcohol use is found to have hepatomegaly and elevated transaminases. His liver disease is described as still potentially reversible at this stage. Which stage in the progression of alcoholic liver disease immediately precedes irreversible cirrhosis?

explanation.summary: Alcoholic liver disease progresses steatosis to steatohepatitis to progressive fibrosis to cirrhosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sequence is steatosis, then steatohepatitis, then progressive fibrosis, and finally cirrhosis; progressive fibrosis is the stage immediately preceding irreversible cirrhosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Steatosis is an early, reversible stage occurring well before cirrhosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Normal histology is not a lesion in the injury sequence leading to cirrhosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatocellular carcinoma is a complication that arises from established cirrhosis, not a precursor stage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acute viral hepatitis is a separate etiology and not the immediate precursor within the alcoholic disease sequence.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old woman with cirrhosis develops new-onset ascites. Her physician recommends abdominal paracentesis even though she has no fever or abdominal pain. What is the primary rationale for performing paracentesis in all patients with new-onset ascites?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To permanently lower portal venous pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: To correct hypoalbuminemia by removing protein-poor fluid

choices.label: D
choices.text: To determine the cause of the ascites and evaluate for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

explanation.summary: Paracentesis in new ascites determines etiology (SAAG) and screens for SBP.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diagnostic paracentesis establishes the cause of ascites via the SAAG and evaluates the fluid for infection (neutrophil count), which is essential because SBP can be present without classic symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Paracentesis removes fluid but does not permanently reduce portal pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It does not correct hypoalbuminemia; large-volume removal can worsen it without albumin replacement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MELD is calculated from blood tests, not from ascitic fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ammonia is measured in serum, not obtained by paracentesis.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C has a rising MELD score, recurrent ascites, and prior variceal bleeding. His disease is described as irreversible. Which of the following is the definitive treatment for his end-stage liver disease?

explanation.summary: Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment for end-stage cirrhosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cirrhosis is irreversible, so aside from managing complications, liver transplantation is the only definitive treatment that replaces the failing organ in end-stage disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-blockers reduce portal pressure and bleeding risk but do not cure the underlying cirrhosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Paracentesis palliates ascites but does not treat the failing liver.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactulose and rifaximin manage encephalopathy, a complication, not the cirrhosis itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Band ligation controls varices but does not reverse or definitively treat end-stage liver disease.
